The UAE's OPEC exit isn't about oil production—quotas were largely ignored anyway. OPEC functions more as a political club than a true cartel, and the UAE's departure signals shifting Gulf politics, not a market shakeup, explains Cato’s Peter Van Doren.

The US indictment of Raul Castro raises hope for an end of the Castro tyranny, something that ideally would happen in a bloodless way, say Cato’s @VasquezIan and @hiperfalcon.

The authoritarian rule of the Cuban Communist Party turned what was once one of Latin America’s most prosperous countries into one of the poorest, a situation that has severely worsened in recent years.

Lawmakers often claim faster economic growth will solve Social Security’s shortfall. But the program is designed so that higher wages mean higher benefits—meaning growth raises costs alongside revenues. Counting on growth isn’t a plan; it’s an excuse to delay real reform.

Secretary of Energy @SecretaryWright at Cato: the path to lower electricity prices, AI leadership, and reindustrialization runs through one thing — fixing the marketplace and letting capitalism work in energy production.

Amid rising energy costs and geopolitical tensions, President Trump issued a temporary waiver of the Jones Act, a century-old law that weakens US shipbuilding and makes everything from energy to groceries more expensive.

In this interview, Cato media fellow @RIKKISCHLOTT sits down with @cpgrabow, associate director at the Cato's Herbert A. Stiefel Center for Trade Policy Studies, to break down the history, economics, and politics of one of America's most damaging protectionist laws.

The DOJ's unsealing of a superseding indictment charging Raúl Castro and five Cuban military pilots is a significant legal and diplomatic event. But criminal indictments of foreign leaders rarely function purely as prosecution vehicles, and the legitimacy of accountability efforts depends in part on whether the standards being invoked are ones we are prepared to apply universally, says Cato’s @ConLawWarrior.

Commemorative passports for America’s 250th anniversary featuring a living president?

Cato’s Dan Greenberg argues public service isn’t self-glorification, and proposes an “Edifice Complex Prevention Act” to curb politicians from branding government projects with their own images.

Virginia prosecutors say the state’s new “assault weapons” ban “cannot be lawfully enforced.” That’s a start—but they may also have standing to sue, based on precedents like Printz and Board of Education v. Allen. Could their lawsuit protect all Virginians? Learn more from Cato’s Matthew Cavedon.

President Trump was distracted by the war with Iran while meeting with Chinese leaders last week. A trade deal isn't enough — if the two sides do not credibly recommit to the "One China" framework, we're just kicking a dangerous can down the road, says Cato’s Evan Sankey.

“The better move would be for President Trump to walk away from the Bank Secrecy Act entirely. That's something the Founders would be proud of,” says Cato’s @EconWithNick.

Secretary Chris Wright discusses how the states that expanded electricity production saw prices rise slower than inflation. States with growing economies and high data center demand are now driving rate freezes and cuts, while other states have rising rates despite using less electricity than they did 10 years ago.
